preamble: The shift from the alveolar nasal [n] to the voiced alveolar stop [d] is a process known as denasalization. It occurs when the velum is raised, blocking nasal airflow while maintaining the same place of articulation. This is often part of a 'strengthening' process in specific prosodic positions. On the Northwest Coast the change is areal: Davidson (2002: 76) describes it for Makah and notes that it also occurred in Ditidaht (Southern Wakashan), Quileute (Chimakuan), and Lushootseed and Twana (Salishan) (pp. 76–77, citing Thompson & Kinkade 1990). In Makah the glottalized nasal *n̓ became d as well.

examples.note: Lushootseed has no phonemic nasals: Proto-Salish *n became d and *m became b; [n] survives only as a speech-style variant of /d/.

examples.to: Northern Sami gieddi, Inari Sami kiedˈdi, Skolt Sami ǩeʹdd
examples.note: Nasal + homorganic stop clusters denasalized to geminate stops (*nt > dd) everywhere except Akkala, Kildin and Ter Sami, which keep the nasal (Kildin кӣннт).

examples.to: Northern Sami goddi, Lule Sami gådde, Inari Sami kodde
examples.note: Kildin коаннҍт and Ter коннҍтӭ keep the nasal.

examples.to: Northern Sami láddi, Inari Sami läddi, Skolt Sami lääʹdd

examples.note: The other Zoquean languages keep the nasal: Sierra Popoluca, Rayón Zoque and Chimalapa Zoque nɨʔ. Wichmann's dataset writes the high central vowel ɨ as ə.

examples.from: Sierra Popoluca (Soteapan) nas, Chiapas Zoque nas 'earth'
Sierra Popoluca nəəyi, Chiapas Zoque nəy 'name'
Sierra Popoluca nəm, Chiapas Zoque nəm 'say'
Sierra Popoluca nəʔəpiñ, Chiapas Zoque nəʔpin 'blood'
examples.note: Texistepec [d] and [b] are in complementary distribution with [n] and [m]: the oral stops occur in onsets and the nasals in codas (Reilly 2002, cited on Wikipedia), so final nasals stay, as in tum 'one' and kaan 'salt'.

languageExamples.context: Davidson (2002: 76): the Proto-Southern-Wakashan nasals became voiced stops in Makah, which accounts for the rarity of m and n there

examples.from: PSW *n, as kept in Nuu-chah-nulth nunu·k 'singing'
Nitinaht (the name as first recorded by Europeans)
examples.note: Wikipedia (Ditidaht language): soon after the name was recorded, m and n shifted to b and d as part of an areal trend, and the people came to call themselves Ditidaht.
